transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-22
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Cortex Head of Platform), Sam Cho (ML Eng), Maya Singh (Security)

Summary: Quick product walkthrough focusing on converting contracts (structured specs) into runtime actions. Demo of JSON mode, schema-driven tool invocation, guardrails in Console, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Customer asked about private deployment and security controls; agreed to pilot and benchmarks.

Topics: Contracts->action mapping, JSON mode schemas, tool calling/fallbacks, runtime guardrails, security (KMS/SAML/SOC2), performance benchmarks, pilot scope

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run through how you can go from a contract/schema to live actions using Redwood. Priya is gonna demo the Console and a short API flow.
[00:18] Alex Rivera: Great, excited. We're mainly focused on reliability and being able to map our internal "policy contracts" into actions that call internal services. We have a on-prem cluster right now and want to see if we should go Hosted, Dedicated, or Private.
[00:30] Priya Patel: Yep, totally. Today we'll show JSON mode with typed responses, how to register an action (tool) that calls your service, and how the runtime enforces schemas and fallbacks. Note: some transcribed names might get munged - apologies for any typos.
[00:45] Sam Cho: Quick question — what's the difference between "tool calling" here and calling a normal webhook?
[00:50] Priya Patel: Good call. Functionally it's a webhook, but we attach typed contracts — so the model must output valid JSON conforming to the schema. The runtime validates and, if required, runs a sandboxed execution path or falls back to a simpler model. That prevents a bad parse and reduces latency from retries.
[01:12] Maya Singh: From security side, we need KMS integration, audit logs, and SAML SSO. Also need to know if PII is ever persisted in the hosted flow.
[01:22] Jordan Kim: We can do KMS/HSM for Private. For Hosted we offer encryption-at-rest and optional customer-managed keys (depending on tier). Audit logs and per-token traces are available in Console. We'll share the SOC2/ISO packet after this call.
[01:36] Alex Rivera: How do you do fallback if the primary model returns invalid JSON? We can't have live incidents.
[01:42] Priya Patel: The runtime has three levers: (1) schema validation with auto-rewrites (we'll attempt a structured correction), (2) model fallback to a more deterministic model variant or lower-latency path, (3) safe sandbox execution — where we run the model output through a lightweight executor that enforces types. You can also configure hard rejections and alerting.
[02:05] [DEMO START] Priya Patel: Ok I'm opening the Redwood Console — top nav, choose "Schemas". Here's the contract Alex showed earlier: action name, input fields (customer_id, consent_flag, payload), expected output enum for status. I'll paste it... (screen shared link: https://console.redwood.ai/demo-sesh)
[02:40] Priya Patel: Now I wire that schema to a tool — Tool: "cortex-verify-service" — endpoint points to a webhook in their VPC via an integration shim (we can show on-prem connector options). I set the retry policy to 1 and fallback behavior to "call-sync-model-only".
[03:05] Sam Cho: When you set fallback to sync-model-only, does it still attempt to call the external service?
[03:09] Priya Patel: No, fallback policies are evaluated on the runtime before the external call is made; if the model can't produce typed output we skip the external call and return the fallback response or route to a quick deterministic model. That prevents cascading failures.
[03:26] Jordan Kim: On performance: typical p50 token latency for the models we demo is ~50-80ms on our hosted rows; p95 varies by sequence length — we usually call out p95 at ~300-600ms for 1k token windows depending on model family. For Dedicated, you can get p50 down and more predictable tail latencies.
[03:56] Alex Rivera: Any examples of cost savings? We care about tokens per dollar.
[04:00] Priya Patel: Redwood Optimize will analyze your workload and recommend batching/prefix caching and quantization profiles. For a token-heavy pipeline we often recommend 4-bit quantization for warm paths and prefix (KV) caching for repeated prompts — customers see 20-60% unit-cost reductions. We'll share a sample Optimize report.
[04:28] [TRANSCRIPTION ERROR] Speaker 1: ...uh the thing about the quantization might —
[04:32] Priya Patel: Sorry, yes. The Optimize module also produces a suggested batch size and expected latency tradeoff table so you can tune for cost or latency.
[04:45] Sam Cho: For the on-prem option, how do you handle model updates and rollouts? We can't have a surprise model swap mid-pilot.
[04:52] Priya Patel: In Private we provide a control plane that you run in your VPC; model artifacts are pulled and pinned per-deployment. Rollouts are canaryed: you can route a percentage to new versions, run A/B, and automatically fallback if QoE metrics regress.
[05:10] Jordan Kim: Alex, did you mention they have a compliance window where audit logs must be retained for 7 years?
[05:15] Alex Rivera: Yes, certain clients demand long-term logs and strict residency.
[05:18] Maya Singh: We also need field-level redaction before any logs leave the VPC.
[05:22] Priya Patel: We support on-host redaction hooks and log suppression for PII. For Private deployments you can configure logs to never leave GRP boundaries; Hosted can be configured with private endpoints and customer-managed keys but may require Dedicated/Enterprise contracts.
[05:42] [DEMO: CONTRACT->ACTION RUN] Priya Patel: I'm executing a test: model receives prompt + schema, returns JSON action: {"action": "verify", "status": "ok", "confidence": 0.98}. Runtime validates, then calls the tool and returns the tool output. If the model returned malformed JSON we show the error and do either auto-correct or fallback.
[06:10] Sam Cho: Do you enable streaming when tools are invoked? We need partial responses for long-running verifications.
[06:16] Priya Patel: Yes, you can stream partial structured responses; however streaming structured JSON requires that the final structure is validated. We emit stream patches and a final validation step; if the final validation fails we can issue a compensating action (e.g., rollback) depending on policy.
[06:35] Alex Rivera: Can we run a pilot where Redwood runs the hosted inference for us, but calls back into our on-prem services? So the models are in Redwood but actions hit our internal APIs.
[06:45] Jordan Kim: That's a common pattern. We call it hybrid routing: model in Redwood hosted, tool endpoints in your VPC through a connector. It preserves data boundaries because payloads can be encrypted in transit with mTLS and routing policies can restrict which actions leave the VPC.
[06:58] Maya Singh: What's the contract around data deletion? If something is flagged we need the ability to scrub it entirely.
[07:03] Priya Patel: We have delete-by-id APIs and can configure no-retention modes for certain customer classes. For Private, you control retention fully.
[07:12] [15-minute mark — demo continues] Priya Patel: I'm switching to a failure simulation — model returns a string instead of JSON. Console shows a validation error, and the runtime suggests an auto-correct using the last-good-schema and a corrective prompt. We then re-run the model with the corrective hint.
[07:48] Sam Cho: Does that corrective prompt leak any internal logic to the model? We want to avoid exposing internal rules if we're sharing prompts.
[07:53] Priya Patel: The corrective prompt is constructed server-side and you can redact sensitive context from it. Also, we log the minimal hint, not the full payload, depending on your logging policy.
[08:06] Alex Rivera: About metrics — can we route traces into our Datadog or Splunk?
[08:10] Jordan Kim: Yes, Redwood Console supports webhook exporters to Datadog and Splunk. We can forward per-request traces, model versions, and token-level cost breakdowns.
[08:20] [Benchmark talk] Priya Patel: When we ran a head-to-head with a common on-prem setup, our Dedicated pool produced roughly 2–3x higher throughput for the same GPU footprint because of our KV cache and attention kernels; you'll find details in the benchmark sheet I linked earlier. Link: https://redwood-internal.sheets/bench-cortex-demo
[08:40] Alex Rivera: We'll need to run that ourselves. Are there any big blockers to running a bench from our dataset?
[08:45] Priya Patel: Not at all — we can ingest a sanitized sample, run a pilot for 2 weeks, and provide a detailed Optimize report. For on-prem privacy we can either run the benchmark in your VPC or run with masked data on our side.
[09:00] [Questions from security] Maya Singh: Are you SOC2 Type II? Also need to see pen-test results.
[09:06] Jordan Kim: Yes, we are SOC2; I'll attach the certs. Pen-test summary and policies are in our security packet. We also support SSO via SAML/OIDC and RBAC with per-route permissions.
[09:20] Sam Cho: For rollout strategy in a pilot, what's recommended? A canary with 5% traffic?
[09:24] Priya Patel: Yes, start with 5% canary for 48–72 hours, watch QoE: p95 latency and reject rate. Then step to 25% and full. Also recommend a synthetic monitor for end-to-end verification.
[09:40] Alex Rivera: If we were to do a Dedicated contract, what's the minimum commitment?
[09:45] Jordan Kim: Typically 3–6 month commitments for Dedicated pools, but we can do a short pilot lease for proof-of-concept. I'll include options in the SOW.
[09:55] [Wrap-up demo examples] Priya Patel: Quick recap of the Console flow: define schema -> register tool -> map schema to tool -> set retry/fallback -> run against dataset -> use Optimize to tune batch/quantization -> monitor via Console.
[10:12] Alex Rivera: That helps. One more: how do you prevent hallucinated tool names or unauthorized actions?
[10:18] Priya Patel: Tools are whitelisted per-schema. The model can't invent a tool name and have the runtime execute it; the runtime only executes a registered tool ID that matches the schema. We also support signed manifests for tool registries.
[10:36] Maya Singh: Nice. That addresses most of our governance questions.
[10:40] Jordan Kim: Ok next steps: Priya will share the Console recording and schema examples; Jordan will send SOW and pilot tiers; Alex will confirm dataset. We'll schedule the benchmark kickoff next week.
[10:55] Alex Rivera: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[11:00] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript: there are occasional mis-attributions and auto-caption artifacts ("on-prem" sometimes transcribed as "on prem"), filler words, and some NLP terms shortened (e.g., "KV cache" into "key visible cache" in one place). Links shared during the call: https://console.redwood.ai/demo-sesh, https://redwood-internal.sheets/bench-cortex-demo

End of transcript.
